plan.contextChunk: This figure places two oblique triangles side by side in plain black outline, lettered identically, to contrast where the altitude lands. In each one the horizontal base is labeled b and runs from the vertex alpha at the left to the vertex gamma at the right, the apex is labeled beta, the short left side from alpha to beta is labeled c, and the long side sloping from beta down to gamma is labeled a. In the left triangle the apex sits above the interior of the base, and a dashed vertical altitude labeled h drops from beta to a point on b, meeting it at a small square marking the right angle; an arc at alpha marks the interior angle. In the right triangle the apex has shifted left beyond alpha, making the angle there obtuse, so the dashed altitude falls outside the figure and the base is carried leftward by a dashed extension to receive its foot. Two arcs appear at that lower left corner, one for the interior angle alpha and, immediately left of it, one for the angle alpha prime between side c and the extension. Setting the arrangements against each other shows that the same height construction serves both, provided the angle used is the one adjacent to the perpendicular, which supplies h for computing the area of a triangle with no right angle of its own.

interactionPlan.concept: To find the height of any oblique triangle, we construct a right triangle by dropping an altitude, which requires extending the base if the adjacent interior angle is obtuse.
elements: horizontal base side b connecting fixed vertices alpha (left) and gamma (right)
movable apex vertex beta
side c connecting alpha and beta
side a connecting beta and gamma
vertex labels alpha, beta, gamma
side labels a, b, c
dashed vertical altitude line dropping from beta to the horizontal base line
label h next to the altitude
right-angle square marker at the foot of the altitude
dashed horizontal extension line continuing left from alpha to meet the altitude
interior angle arc at alpha
exterior angle arc between side c and the extended base, labeled alpha prime (visible when apex is left of alpha)

interactions.label: Apex position
interactions.teaches: Moving the apex horizontally across the lower-left vertex shows the continuous transition from an acute to an obtuse triangle, forcing the altitude outside the figure.

interactions.label: Altitude construction
interactions.teaches: Revealing the altitude connects the oblique triangle to a right-triangle height calculation, which requires extending the base when the angle is obtuse.

demo_steps.title: The oblique triangle
demo_steps.narration: To compute the area of a triangle, we need a perpendicular height. But this oblique triangle has no right angle of its own.

demo_steps.title: Dropping the altitude
demo_steps.narration: By constructing a perpendicular altitude from the apex to the base, we form a right triangle. For an acute angle at alpha, this altitude falls inside the base.

demo_steps.title: The obtuse case
demo_steps.narration: If the apex shifts so that the angle at alpha becomes obtuse, the altitude falls outside the triangle. We extend the base and use the adjacent supplementary angle (alpha prime) to calculate the height.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The right triangle used to calculate the altitude always sits adjacent to the vertex, even if it has to fall outside the triangle along an extended base line.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Draw a single interactive triangle. Base b is horizontal and fixed between alpha and gamma. Apex beta moves horizontally based on the apexPosition slider. When beta is to the right of alpha (slider > 0), altitude h drops onto b. When beta is to the left of alpha (slider < 0), altitude h drops outside, base b is extended leftward with a dashed line to meet it, and the exterior angle alpha prime arc and label appear. Use clear black outlines and italic serif labels for variables.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for moving vertex beta: the learner drags the apex horizontally across alpha, the altitude foot moves from inside the base to outside on the dashed extension, showing why the height construction changes position for acute versus obtuse arrangements.
- Toggle between acute and obtuse angle views: the learner switches the named case, the base extension and alpha prime label appear only in the obtuse view, making clear which adjacent angle supplies the perpendicular height.
- Click for altitude construction: the learner clicks side b, a dashed perpendicular h drops from beta and the right-angle marker appears, connecting the oblique triangle to the right-triangle height used in area calculations.

authoredContext:
Now that we can solve a triangle for missing values, we can use some of those values and the sine function to find the area of an oblique triangle. Recall that the area formula for a triangle is given as Area= 1 2 bh, where b is base and h is height. For oblique triangles, we must find h before we can use the area formula. Observing the two triangles in the figure, one acute and one obtuse, we can drop a perpendicular to represent the height and then apply the trigonometric property sinα= opposite hypotenuse to write an equation for area in oblique triangles. In the acute triangle, we have sinα= h c or csinα=h. However, in the obtuse triangle, we drop the perpendicular outside the triangle and extend the base b to form a right triangle. The angle used in calculation is α ′, or 180−α.

Two oblique triangles with standard labels. Both have a dotted altitude line h extended from angle beta to the horizontal base side b. In the first, which is an acute triangle, the altitude is within the triangle. In the second, which is an obtuse triangle, the altitude h is outside of the triangle.

The Greek letter labels are italicized, whereas standard math formatting and the source figure use upright Greek letters.

Remove the `italic` font styling from the Greek letter labels (α, β, γ, α') to match the upright mathematical formatting seen in the source.
